title: You Don't Have to Live in the District You Represent
hook: The Constitution asks a House candidate to be an inhabitant of the state — not the district. That gap is why 'carpetbagger' is an insult and not a disqualification.
key_points: Article I requires a U.S. House member to be 25, a citizen for seven years, and an inhabitant of the state when elected.
There is no federal requirement to live in the specific district — a candidate can move in weeks before filing.
States cannot add qualifications of their own; the Supreme Court held the constitutional list is a ceiling, not a floor.
'Carpetbagger' dates to Reconstruction, for outsiders said to arrive with everything they owned in a cheap bag.
NPR reports six former congressional hopefuls from other states running in one Southwest Florida GOP primary.
content_html: Every so often a congressional race turns into an argument about a candidate's mailing address. The charge is "carpetbagging": you moved here to run, you are not really one of us. It is a potent political attack, and it is almost never a legal problem — because the Constitution sets a lower bar than voters often assume.
extra_html: Article I lists exactly three qualifications for the House: be at least 25, a citizen for at least seven years, and an inhabitant of the state you are elected in. Nothing requires living in the district itself, and nothing sets a minimum length of residence, so a candidate can relocate shortly before filing and still qualify. States have tried to tighten this and lost; the Supreme Court has treated the constitutional list as exclusive, meaning a state may not bolt extra requirements onto federal office. The result is that the question gets settled politically rather than legally — voters decide whether local roots matter. NPR's Maham Javaid reports a vivid illustration in Southwest Florida, where a conservative-stronghold House primary drew six people who had previously run for Congress in other states. The word for it goes back to Reconstruction, when Northerners heading South were caricatured as arriving with all their belongings in a carpet-fabric bag.

related.title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
related.hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

related.title: Districts & Gerrymandering
related.hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

related.title: What Citizenship Is
related.hook: Citizenship is the formal bond between a person and a state — the status that turns a resident into a full member, with rights and duties to match.

flashcards.prompt: What residency does the Constitution require of a U.S. House candidate?

choices.text: Inhabitant of the state when elected — the district is not specified
Resident of the specific district for at least five years
Birth in the district they seek to represent

flashcards.explanation_html: Article I sets age, citizenship, and state inhabitancy. District residency is a political expectation, not a legal one.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't a state simply require its House candidates to live in the district?
flashcards.back_html: Because the Supreme Court has treated the Constitution's list of qualifications as exclusive — states may not add to it.

flashcards.prompt: What does the term 'carpetbagger' originally refer to?

choices.text: A Reconstruction-era outsider said to show up carrying all they owned in a cheap bag
A campaign donor who gives only in cash
A candidate who refuses to debate

flashcards.explanation_html: The insult targets the perceived opportunism of arriving from elsewhere to seek office — a charge about legitimacy, not legality.
